concept.name: Confidence interval
concept.definition: An interval estimate for a population parameter constructed so that a stated proportion (the confidence level, e.g., 95%) of intervals built the same way from repeated samples would contain the true parameter value. For the mean with unknown variance it uses the t distribution with N - 1 degrees of freedom.
concept.intuition: Instead of one best-guess number, it gives a plausible range whose width communicates how uncertain the estimate is: narrow means precise, wide means noisy.
concept.mechanics: For a mean: take the sample mean plus and minus a t critical value times the standard error s/sqrt(N). The width is driven by sample size (1/sqrt(N)) and by the data's standard deviation; the confidence level 1 - alpha is set before computing (commonly 0.95).
concept.formula: Y_bar +/- t_{1-alpha/2, N-1} * s / sqrt(N), where Y_bar is the sample mean, s the sample standard deviation, N the sample size, and t the percentile of the t distribution with N-1 degrees of freedom at confidence level 1 - alpha.
concept.failure_modes: The stated coverage assumes the sampling model (independence, approximate normality of the mean) holds; autocorrelated or heavy-tailed returns produce intervals with true coverage below the nominal level. Intervals also inherit any bias in how the data were collected (e.g., survivorship bias in fund samples).
concept.misconceptions: A 95% confidence interval does NOT mean there is a 95% probability that this particular interval contains the true mean - it either does or does not; the 95% refers to the long-run success rate of the method across repeated samples (a point NIST states explicitly).
concept.example: With N = 195, mean 9.2615, s = 0.0228, and t = 1.972, NIST computes a 95% CI of (9.2582, 9.2647); because 5 lies outside it, H0: mu = 5 is rejected at the 5% level - the duality between intervals and tests.
